html:
On 12 October 1492, ships under Christopher Columbus sighted land in the Bahamas, an island its Taíno people called Guanahani. This landing began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.

Columbus had sailed from Palos in southern Spain in August with three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, backed by Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon. He was looking for a western sea route to Asia. After stopping in the Canary Islands, the crossing took about five weeks. From the Bahamas he sailed on to Cuba and Hispaniola. When the Santa María ran aground, he left 39 men in a fort on Hispaniola and went home to a hero's welcome in early 1493.

Columbus believed he had reached the Indies near Asia, which is why Caribbean peoples were called "Indians" and the islands the West Indies. Within a few years, others such as Amerigo Vespucci argued these were new lands, and the Americas were later named after him.

The results were enormous and grim. The voyage opened the Columbian Exchange: maize, potatoes and tobacco went east, while horses, wheat, sugar and European diseases came west. The Taíno of Hispaniola were nearly wiped out within decades by disease, forced labour and violence. In 1494 Spain and Portugal split the newly found world between them, and the conquests of Spanish America followed. Many historians date the start of the modern era to this landing.
sum: On 12 October 1492, ships under Christopher Columbus sighted land in the Bahamas, an island its Taíno people called Guanahani. This landing began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.
